title: Moth Eye
hook: Hide a moth’s shiny eye from the bat.
sub: Real moth eyes kill glare with nanopillars. Put a 3D nanopillar eye under the loupe, shade it with a quantum thin-film shader, stack up to six layers, and see whether the bat still spots the shine.
you_control: Orbit the 3D eye in the loupe (drag, pinch, arrow keys); the bat flies to your viewing angle
Move the lamp on the light pad or by dragging the sky
Stack layers 1-6 (each a real shader run); switch the nonlinear interaction off at 1 and 6
Compare moth eye, bare dome and flat slab; sweep the viewing tilt
qubits_note: 6 layers x 6 rays is the largest stack the engine accepts: 7 rays at 6 layers was rejected ('at most 6'), 7+ layers allow at most 5 rays but need rays >= layers; each ray is one qubit, so 6x6 = 21. Smaller runs ~17-20 qubits from our fit q = rays + layers - floor(layers/4) + 10 to the engine's budget messages (engine reports no per-job count).
deliverables: web/video/moth_eye.mp4 (smaller H.264 copy of the film, played on the page)
out/jobs/ (8 engine ZIPs: GLSL/HLSL/OSL/.frag/MaterialX + R/T EXR/HDR LUTs)
make_plates.py (the engraved plates: hawkmoth head, facet inset, big brown bat, lamp, bat-head meter, Plates I and II)
web/sprites.json (the mascot sprite, rasterised from the head plate)
honesty: Analogy only: real moth eyes are sub-wavelength graded-index; the engine models a thin conducting-sheet stack on Atlas's classical statevector simulator, and in it more layers raise reflectance (0.418 -> 0.479) rather than kill it.
